tour.title: Fairy Chimneys, Rock Churches & the Valleys
tour.summary: A ground-level day in Cappadocia: Byzantine frescoes cut into the rock, the fairy chimneys that give the region its name, and a walk through Rose and Red valleys to the sunset rim.
tour.overviewText:
Cappadocia does not look like anywhere else on earth, and nobody built it. Between roughly three and nine million years ago, volcanoes — Erciyes, Hasan Dağı and Göllüdağ — buried this plateau in ash. Ash that settles while still hot can weld into a rock called tuff: soft enough to scratch with a fingernail, strong enough to stand as a wall. Later eruptions capped it with harder stone. Then rain, frost and wind went to work, and wherever a hard block sat on softer ash it sheltered a column beneath. That is a fairy chimney — peri bacası in Turkish, "fairy's chimney" — and this whole region is a city of them.

People have carved the soft rock since at least the third century, and for a thousand years the valleys around Göreme were monastic. Basil of Caesarea, one of the fourth-century theologians Christians call a Cappadocian Father, urged men and women to withdraw into the rock; they cut cells, refectories and churches, and when Arab armies raided across Anatolia from the seventh century they dug whole cities underground to hide in. The churches you will enter were painted after the iconoclast controversy — two Byzantine campaigns of image-banning, in 726–787 and 814–842, when crosses replaced figures — so the frescoes belong to the triumphant return of images after 843, which is why the best of them look almost newly painted.

Politics then emptied the valleys. In 1923, after the Greco-Turkish war, Greece and Turkey agreed to swap their minorities by religion: about 1.2 million Greek Orthodox Christians left Anatolia for Greece, and roughly 400,000 Muslims went the other way. Cappadocia's Christians were among them — many Turkish-speaking, their books printed in Turkish using the Greek alphabet, a script called Karamanlidika. Their churches stopped being churches and a landscape of living faith became an archaeological one — which is also why the frescoes survived: nobody was left to paint over them.

Today Cappadocia is a tourism economy. The Seljuks and Ottomans who ruled here after 1071 left their own layer — medreses, the Islamic colleges of the medieval Turkish world, still stand in nearby towns — but the modern story is balloons and cave hotels. In 2025 nearly 754,000 people flew over these valleys. Tourism brought wealth and emptied the village: almost every old cave house has been rebuilt, and most residents now work in the industry or have moved.

The walk itself is a loop through the heart of it. It starts at the museum gate east of the village, drops back through the fairy chimneys, climbs to the sunset ridge, then turns north into Rose Valley and follows the trail between rock-cut churches and old vineyards to finish on the Red Valley rim at golden hour — about 7.5 km of walking, spread over a full day, with two to three hours on your feet inside the museum.

Practically: wear shoes with grip, carry more water than feels necessary, and treat the valley trails as footpaths — unmarked, unshaded and loose underfoot. Museum tickets run to a few hundred lira and rise yearly, so verify at the gate; the trails are free.

This is Cappadocia from the ground up. Walk it slowly; the rock has been patient for millions of years and rewards the same.
tour.difficulty: Moderate, and a full day. Paved streets and a wide museum path, then unmarked dirt trails in Rose and Red valleys with loose gravel, rock steps and no shade. About 7.5 km of walking — roughly two hours in motion — plus two to three hours on your feet inside the museum. Sturdy shoes and water are essential.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start at the museum gate when it opens (08:00) to beat the coaches, walk back through the village, then save the valleys for the afternoon: the Rose Valley cliffs glow in the two hours before sunset and Red Valley is the region's classic sunset perch. For balloons, come to the sunset point at dawn on another morning — they launch at first light and the wind decides.

stops.name: Göreme Open Air Museum
stops.narration:
A kilometre or so east of the village, a valley of rock cones holds the densest collection of painted churches in Cappadocia. This is the Göreme Open Air Museum — açık hava müzesi, literally "open-air museum" — and since 1985 it has sat inside a UNESCO World Heritage Site listed as Göreme National Park and the Rock Sites of Cappadocia. There is no building to enter. The site is the cliff.

Start with the rock. The whole landscape is tuff — volcanic ash that fell from Erciyes and Hasan Dağı and welded into a soft stone you could carve with a chisel, or, as the monks did, with a spoon and patience. Harder flows capped it. Water found the cracks, frost widened them, and the softer ash retreated into cones and gullies. The monks did not have to quarry: they had only to hollow.

Christianity arrived early and took to the rock. In the fourth century Basil, bishop of Caesarea — one of the Cappadocian Fathers, the theologians who shaped Christian doctrine on the Trinity — urged ascetics to withdraw into communities of prayer and work. They cut cells and chapels straight into the valley walls. When Arab armies began raiding across Anatolia in the seventh century, the same soft rock let them vanish: they dug multi-storey underground cities, some reaching eighty metres down, with rolling stone doors. The valleys you are walking were, for centuries, a monastic countryside.

Look at the churches for a lesson in Byzantine politics. Between roughly 726 and 787, and again from 814 to 842, the Byzantine state banned religious images in a movement historians call iconoclasm — icon-breakers, from the Greek for "image" and "to break". Church walls were reduced to crosses and geometry. Then in 843 the ban collapsed, images returned, and painters made up for lost time. The frescoes here — flat, vivid, more diagram than portrait, with every figure labelled — belong to that return. This is why Cappadocian painting looks so confident: it was painted by people who had just won the argument.

The circuit has a handful of must-sees. Tokalı Kilise, the Buckle Church, is the largest, with a ninth- to tenth-century nave and an eleventh-century extension whose deep indigo blues were ground from lapis lazuli carried from Afghanistan — pigment worth its weight in gold. Elmalı Kilise, the Apple Church, is small and domed. Yılanlı Kilise, the Snake Church, shows Saint George killing the dragon and, unusually, the emperor Constantine with his mother Helena holding the True Cross. Çarıklı Kilise, the Sandal Church, is named for two footprints painted below the Ascension.

Then pay the extra for the Dark Church — Karanlık Kilise — and go in slowly. Built in the eleventh century with only one small window in its narthex, it stayed so dim that its frescoes kept their colour for a thousand years. Christ Pantocrator in the dome, the Nativity, the Last Supper, the Crucifixion, the Anastasis: this is the best-preserved Byzantine painting in Cappadocia. It survived partly by accident — after the Christians left, it served as a pigeon house until the 1950s, and workers spent years scraping away the droppings. Which is also the story of the whole site: these churches were in use until 1923, when the Greek Orthodox Christians of Cappadocia were expelled to Greece in the population exchange, and the valleys went quiet.

Practicalities: the main ticket has lately run around 480 Turkish lira (₺), with the Dark Church on a separate ticket of roughly 130–200 ₺ or €6, and the Museum Pass is not valid for the Dark Church. Prices climb with inflation most years — verify at the gate. Summer hours are roughly 08:00–19:00, winter shorter, and the Dark Church closes earlier, around 16:45 with last sales at 16:00. Come at opening to dodge the coach groups. No flash inside the churches, and no touching the paint.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Main ticket has lately been about 480 ₺, with the Dark Church a separate 130–200 ₺ (or €6); the Museum Pass is not valid for the Dark Church. Turkish museum prices rise most years — verify at the gate and carry small notes.
stops.openingHours: Roughly 08:00–19:00 daily in summer, shorter in winter. The Dark Church closes earlier — about 16:45, with last ticket sales around 16:00. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Partly accessible, honestly: the main loop is a wide gravel and paved path with gentle slopes, but the churches are reached by steep, uneven stone steps and low doorways, and the Dark Church entrance is narrow. Not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Arrive at opening (08:00) — the coach groups land mid-morning, and a tiny church shared with thirty people is no fun. Then go straight to the Dark Church while it is still empty, and let your eyes adjust for a full minute before you judge the frescoes.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the museum gate and walk back west along Müze Caddesi toward the village, about a kilometre and a half and twenty minutes on a gentle downhill road. As the buildings close in around you, the roadside is suddenly full of rock cones and cave fronts — that is the next stop, the fairy chimneys of Göreme itself.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Bernard Gagnon, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Fairy Chimneys of Göreme
stops.narration:
You are standing among the things the postcards are made of. Around the village the soft rock has eroded into cones, tents and towers, each one wearing a harder stone hat. In Turkish they are peri bacaları — "fairy chimneys" — though geologists, who dislike fairies, call them hoodoos. The name matters less than the mechanism, and the mechanism is simple enough to see.

Picture the sequence. Ash and lava flow out of a volcano and settle in layers, some soft, some hard. Water cuts gullies down the slope. Where a hard boulder or a thick lava band happens to sit on top of soft tuff, it acts as an umbrella: the rain runs around the column instead of through it, and the cone beneath is spared while everything around it is washed away. The capstone is the whole trick. Knock it off — and it does fall, eventually — and the exposed cone dissolves in a geological instant. You can read the life cycle in a single slope: fat cones with intact hats, skinny ones losing them, and stumps.

People moved in. Until a generation ago, families here lived in the rock itself: a carved cave for sleeping, a stone room built in front, caves behind used as stables and storerooms. Look for the small square holes in the valley walls — pigeon houses, guano farms, where droppings were collected to fertilise the vineyards. Look, too, for flat rock floors scored with shallow channels: grape-treading presses, cut when wine was the valley's cash crop.

That way of life has almost gone. From the 1970s, and decisively in the 2000s, tourism arrived. Almost every old cave house in Göreme has been sold and rebuilt as a boutique hotel; the villagers who owned them often moved out to Nevşehir, Ürgüp or Avanos. The people you see in the streets are mostly visitors, and the people serving them commute in. Tourism pays better than farming ever did, and it has hollowed the village as surely as it filled it. Supporters call it renewal; critics mourn a community that sold its own houses. Both are describing the same street.

One practical rule: do not climb the chimneys. The rock is soft, the cones are old, and a foothold you break today will not grow back. Wander, photograph, and keep your hands off the fairy hats.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free — these are public streets and slopes in and around the village. Nothing to pay, but do not climb the cones; the rock is fragile and it damages easily.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Best in morning or late-afternoon light, when the cones cast long shadows.
stops.accessibility: The village streets are paved but narrow and often steep, with steps between terraces; the slopes among the chimneys are uneven dirt. Not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Look for the pigeon-house holes and the grape-treading basins cut into the rock — easy to mistake for natural holes, and they explain how the valley fed itself for centuries.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the town centre, walk east and then south-east for ten or fifteen minutes, following the steep stepped lane up to the hilltop with the Turkish flag. That is the sunset point — Aydın Kırağı, also called Lovers' Hill. It is a short climb but a sharp one; take it slowly in the heat.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Feridun F. Alkaya, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Göreme Sunset Point (Aydın Kırağı)
stops.narration:
Climb the stairs and turn around: the whole town is below you, a scatter of flat roofs and cones, and beyond it the valleys fold away toward Uçhisar, whose castle is a single tuff pinnacle hollowed into rooms. Locals call this hill Aydın Kırağı, and many visitors call it Lovers' Hill — Aşıklar Tepesi. There is a Turkish flag on the summit and a small kiosk at the bottom that charges a few lira to pass; it changes, so keep coins.

You are standing on the rim of the same system you have been walking through, and from up here you can see how it was made. The valleys run like veins because water made them: rain gathers, cuts a channel, and the channel deepens into a canyon with cones left standing on the shoulders. The pale bands in the cliffs are separate ash flows — each one an eruption, cooled and compressed into tuff. The dark bands are harder rock that resisted. Erosion did not happen once; it is happening now, every winter.

If you are here at dawn, you are here for the balloons. Cappadocia runs the largest commercial balloon operation on earth: 754,098 passengers flew in 2025, and on an average morning about 156 balloons rise over these valleys. They launch at first light because that is when the air is calmest — and calm is not a preference but a rule. A hot-air balloon has no steering. The pilot can only heat the air to rise, vent it to fall, and pick a wind layer going the way they want; the whole flight is a negotiation with the weather. So Turkey's civil aviation authority, the SHGM, sends inspectors out before dawn to read wind speed, visibility, cloud base and rain, and decides how many balloons, or whether any, may fly. A wind of about ten knots at launch is enough to ground the fleet. If your own flight was cancelled for high wind, this is why — and why no operator can promise you a flight on any given morning. The compensation is a hill like this, which costs almost nothing and shows you the same sunrise.

The view also explains the economy. Balloons, cave hotels, guided tours and the museum you just left are what Cappadocia sells now, and they are why a village of two thousand people has hotels for many times that number. It is a landscape that pays its way by being looked at — which is both its protection, since visitors pay for its upkeep, and its risk, since visitors wear it down.

Give it twenty minutes, or an hour at sunset when the tuff turns amber. Then head north along the ridge road toward the Rose Valley trailhead; the path leaves town at the top end, and the signposts are small.
stops.entranceFeeNote: A small local entry fee — reported at a few lira and creeping up with inflation; keep small notes. The hill is otherwise free, unlike the private balloon-viewing terraces.
stops.openingHours: Open through the day; busiest at sunrise (balloons) and sunset. The kiosk keeps daylight hours.
stops.accessibility: Not accessible: a steep stepped lane and uneven rock at the top, slippery when dusty or wet. Sturdy shoes and a slow pace.
stops.insiderTip: Come at dawn on a clear morning, not just at sunset — this is the cheapest front-row seat for the balloon launch, and the light on the valleys is best in the first twenty minutes after sunrise.
stops.nextStopDirections: Come back down into town and head for the north end, following the road that leaves Göreme toward Çavuşin. Walk about two kilometres north — twenty-five minutes or so — until the houses thin out and a dirt path drops into a gap between cliffs on your right, marked by a small, easily missed sign. That is the Rose Valley trailhead. If in doubt, ask for Güllüdere.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Dosseman, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Rose Valley Trailhead (Güllüdere)
stops.narration:
This is the mouth of Rose Valley — Güllüdere in Turkish — and it is the doorway into the walk that everyone comes to Cappadocia for. You are about two kilometres north of Göreme, on the road toward the village of Çavuşin, and from here a dirt path drops between two walls of rock and heads up-valley. There is no gate, no ticket, and no one to ask. That is the point, and also the warning.

First, the name. At the end of the day these cliffs glow rose and orange, and the colour is not a trick of the light alone. The tuff here is rich in iron, and when iron in rock meets air and water it rusts into the red and pink oxides you can see streaking the walls. Different ash layers hold different amounts of it, so the valley is banded — pale grey where a flow was poor in iron, deep rose where it was rich. When the low sun rakes across the bands, the whole valley seems lit from inside.

Now look at what the rock was used for. Those ledges and holes along the cliffs are not natural. Cappadocia has grown vines for millennia — the Hittites made wine here, and the Greek-speaking villagers who lived in these valleys until 1923 kept the tradition going. Look for the flat, shallow-cut basins in the rock: treading floors, where grapes were crushed by foot, the juice running down a channel into a sunken vat. Nearby, families cut presses and storerooms. Wine was not a luxury here; it was a household industry, and the valleys were its vineyards. The industry has come back — there are wineries around Ürgüp and Uçhisar now — but the old rock cellars are the older chapter.

A few honest words before you set off. This is a working footpath, not a theme park. There is almost no shade, the ground is loose gravel and dust, and the junctions are marked, if at all, by faded paint. Take more water than you think you need, wear shoes with grip, and do not start late enough to be caught by darkness in an unfamiliar valley — people do, and the rescue is embarrassing and occasionally worse. Snakes and scorpions exist; they want nothing to do with you, so watch where you put your hands and feet rather than worrying about them.

Then walk in. The path climbs gently between the cliffs, and the first churches are ten or fifteen minutes ahead.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free — it is a public footpath, with no gate or ticket. Any church that asks for a small fee is charging for its upkeep and access, not admission to the valley.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times; walk it in daylight. Best from mid-afternoon so the cliffs are lit for the return.
stops.accessibility: Not accessible: dirt and loose gravel paths, uneven rock steps into the churches, no handrails. The first stretch is gentle, but the valley is not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Take a litre of water per person and start no later than mid-afternoon. There is almost no shade and the junctions are only faintly marked — a photo of the trail sign at the start is cheap insurance.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the trailhead, take the dirt path into the valley and follow it uphill between the cliffs. After ten or fifteen minutes the first carved facades appear on your left and right. Keep going up-valley — the main churches, Direkli and Haçlı, are another twenty minutes or so — and look for the long refectories nearby. There is no single route; stay on the main path and let the rock guide you.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Zeynel Cebeci, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Rose & Red Valley Trail
stops.narration:
Now the valley does what the valley does. Follow the path and you pass one carved facade after another — some are stables and storerooms, some are houses, and some are churches with painted interiors that have been dark for seven centuries. This was not wilderness. It was a monastic neighbourhood, and it was busy.

The churches come with names that describe them. Direkli Kilise, the Church of Columns — also called Kolonlu — has columns cut from the living rock, as if a mason had quarried a basilica in place and left the pillars standing. Haçlı Kilise, the Church of the Cross, is laid out as a Greek cross, and in its early layer the decoration is exactly that: crosses, no faces. You are looking at iconoclasm again — the Byzantine ban on images — and this church is a good place to see its footprint, because later hands added figures on top. Üzümlü Kilise, the Grape Church, is named for the vine and grape motifs painted across its walls; in one scene you can find a stylised bunch of grapes, the old sign of the Eucharist, the bread-and-wine ritual at the centre of Christian worship. Nearby, whole monastic complexes survive: long refectories with rock-cut tables and benches, where the community ate together, and kitchens, storage rooms and cells behind.

Notice, too, the little square holes punched high in the cliff face, dozens at a time. Those are pigeon houses. Pigeons were kept deliberately, not casually: their droppings are a rich fertiliser, and farmers collected them from these niches to spread on the vineyards below. The birds were the valley's fertiliser factory, and the guano trade is one of the quiet reasons the vines survived in thin volcanic soil.

Look around at the terraces and you can still see the vine rows, and the ruined walls of what were once garden plots and small houses. The people who farmed these terraces were Greek Orthodox Christians — many of them Turkish-speaking, their books printed in Turkish using the Greek alphabet, a script called Karamanlidika. They worshipped in these churches, buried their dead in the rock, and were expelled to Greece in the 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey. The churches have been empty ever since. Some were converted into mosques or used as barns; most simply waited. What saved the paintings is the same thing that saved the Dark Church — darkness, and nobody bothering to scrub them off.

A few churches are looked after by a café or a caretaker who may ask for a small fee or expect you to buy a tea; others are open and free. Carry a torch — phone light is enough for most, but the paint is easier to see in soft, angled light than in a harsh beam. Do not touch the frescoes; the pigment sits on a thin plaster and the oil on your fingers is enough to lift it. And if a doorway is chained, respect it: some of these buildings are fragile, and a few have conservation work in progress. The trail continues down-valley toward the Red Valley, where the walls turn a deeper red and the path climbs to the viewpoint.
stops.entranceFeeNote: The trail is free. A few churches are managed by a nearby café or caretaker who may ask a small fee or expect a purchase; others are simply open. Verify on the spot.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times; visit in daylight. The trail is best in the two or three hours before sunset, when the rock is lit and the heat has gone.
stops.accessibility: Not accessible: rough dirt trail, loose scree, rock steps and low, narrow church doorways. A torch helps inside. Not step-free, and not for anyone unsteady on their feet.
stops.insiderTip: In the churches, switch off your flash and wait a minute for your eyes to adjust — the paint reads far better in dim, angled light than under a phone torch. And hunt the grape motifs in Üzümlü Kilise.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the churches, follow the trail down-valley as it bends toward the redder walls; where paths fork, keep to the wider one heading south-west and uphill toward the rim. After fifteen or twenty minutes the path climbs out onto the ridge and the Red Valley viewpoint opens in front of you. If you lose the trail, aim for the ridge with the parked cars and the café.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: prilfish, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Red Valley Viewpoint (Kızıl Vadi)
stops.narration:
The last light is the reason this valley has two names. Rose Valley turns pink at dusk; Red Valley — Kızıl Vadi — turns the colour of embers. You are standing on its rim, and the cliffs in front of you are the same tuff you have walked through all day, stained deep red by iron oxide. As the sun drops, the banding sharpens: pale ash flow, dark resistant band, pale again, each one an eruption that happened millions of years ago and is only now being taken apart by the weather.

Step back and see the whole machine. Erciyes, the great volcano near Kayseri, still stands 3,917 metres high; Hasan Dağı, the other, rises to the south-west. For millions of years they blanketed this plateau in ash and lava. Ash that settles hot can weld into tuff; ash that settles cool stays loose and washes away. Eruptions came in waves, so the plateau is a layer cake of welded and loose material, and erosion — rain, frost, the freeze-thaw of a thousand winters — has eaten the loose layers and left the welded ones standing as cones, walls and mesas. Geologists have listed the Cappadocian ignimbrites among the world's hundred most important geological heritage sites, which is a formal way of saying this landscape is a textbook.

There is a darker note in the rock, and it is real. The tuff around some Cappadocian villages contains erionite, a mineral fibre similar to asbestos, and in the twentieth century three villages nearby suffered catastrophically high rates of mesothelioma, a cancer of the lung lining. The cause turned out to be both the mineral and a genetic susceptibility in certain families. It is a reminder that this beautiful soft stone is not harmless, and that the people who lived in it paid a price the postcards never show.

Now look out and count the balloons, if the morning was calm. On a good day about 156 of them rise over these valleys; in 2025 nearly three-quarters of a million people flew. That is the modern Cappadocia in one image — a landscape so strange that the best way to see it is to float over it. But you have done the older thing: you have walked it. You have stood in churches cut by hand, read the geology in the cliffs, and followed the path the villagers took to their vineyards.

The tourism that fills these valleys is the same force that emptied the cave houses and turned them into hotels. It is neither simply good nor simply bad: it pays for the museums and the trails, and it wears them down. What you can do is small and concrete — stay on the path, keep your hands off the paint, buy from the people who live here, and leave the rock as you found it. The fairy chimneys took millions of years to make. They are not in a hurry, and neither should you be.
stops.entranceFeeNote: The viewpoint itself is free; some operators charge a small parking or terrace fee if you arrive by car. On foot there is usually nothing to pay. Verify if asked.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times; the whole point is the last hour before sunset. Do not linger after dark on the unlit trail.
stops.accessibility: The rim is reached by a rough uphill trail with loose stone; the viewpoint itself is uneven rock and dirt. Not step-free, and not for anyone unsteady on their feet, especially after dark.
stops.insiderTip: Stay ten minutes past sunset. The cliffs keep their red for a few minutes after the sun has gone and most people leave too early — but work out your route back to the road before the light fails.
stops.nextStopDirections: This is the end of the walk. The easiest way back to Göreme is to follow the ridge road west toward the village — about forty minutes on foot — or take a taxi; the dolmuş, the shared minibus that links the Cappadocian villages, does not come up here, so do not wait for one. If you have time, stay for the last of the light, then walk back into town, find a bowl of testi kebap — the local stew baked in a sealed clay pot that you crack open at the table — and call it a day.
